demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself
make sure to stay close to exit

Threat.value: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again

Memory.value: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
When I remember the event I feel intense shame

Negative Appraisals.value: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.explanation: Occupation 'Retired' is implausible for age 30 because 'Retired' is only considered plausible at age 50 or older.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: The appraisal of betrayal by a trusted person is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another, unless there were additional interpersonal-trauma elements not represented elsewhere. It pulls the profile toward betrayal/interpersonal trauma rather than guilt-based accidental harm.

issues.item: Triggers: Authority Commands: Being given orders or instructions
issues.explanation: The trigger set centers on authority commands and family-related cues, which is possible but not well supported by the rest of the profile. With accidental injury to another, the most coherent triggers would usually connect to the accident context, harm, guilt, or responsibility; these selected cues lack a clear link to the memory and appraisal content presented.

issues.item: Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family
issues.explanation: Family-related comments and idealized families imply loss, parenting/family injury, or comparison with intact families, but no corresponding memory or appraisal item explains why family cues are central. This makes the trigger pattern feel disconnected rather than tightly linked to the rest of the profile.

The threat items describe pervasive danger monitoring for attack or violence across all environments, which fits assault/combat formulations better than accidentally injuring someone. They are difficult to connect to the selected memories, which emphasize vividness, disorganization, and shame rather than danger from external perpetrators.

The trigger set is centered on family/loss themes, which fits bereavement- or family-related trauma more than accidentally causing serious injury to another. For this trauma type, such triggers are hard to reconcile unless the injured person was a family member, which is not indicated elsewhere in the profile.

The threat items reflect a pervasive danger/assault formulation (scanning exits, noticing weapons, on guard at home) rather than the likely core threat in perpetration-by-accident trauma, which is more often moral threat, fear of blame, or fear of causing harm again. These threat items are difficult to connect to the selected triggers and appraisals.

Within the formulation, Threat strongly drives Maladaptive Strategies, so a strategy like staying near exits should be tightly linked to a plausible danger-based threat profile. Because the threat content itself is poorly matched to the trauma type and other nodes, 'Stay Near Exit' also appears incoherent in this profile.

The trigger profile is centered on guilt/loss reminders (happy families, talk about losing loved ones, alcohol smell), which fits accidentally causing serious injury to another. In contrast, the threat items are dominated by generalized interpersonal/physical danger hypervigilance (scanning exits, noticing weapons, on guard at home), a pattern more typical of assault/combat trauma than guilt-based accidental injury.

issues.item: Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: 'Stay near exit' mirrors the same pervasive danger/escape theme as the threat items, but the rest of the profile—especially negative appraisals and memory—focuses on shame, guilt, and disorganized vivid recall of having harmed someone. This creates a cross-node mismatch: the coping and threat responses address an ongoing attack-danger context not otherwise represented in the trauma meaning.

issues.item: Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
issues.explanation: Given the formulation, Triggers strongly connect to Memory, Negative Appraisals, and Maladaptive Strategies, with only weak Triggers → Threat. The selected trigger items plausibly evoke shame/loss memories, but they do not clearly connect to the severe omnipresent danger threat pattern endorsed. That weakens coherence between node content and the edge pattern.

issues.item: Triggers: Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
issues.explanation: For trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another, the trigger about 'people losing loved ones' is a poor fit unless the injured person died or there was bereavement trauma; it conflicts with the specified trauma type of serious injury rather than death.

issues.item: Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
issues.explanation: The threat profile centers on generalized physical-danger/hypervigilance ('on guard even inside my own home', 'noticing weapons in any environment'), which is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile that is dominated by guilt, shame, and event-related recall after having caused injury to another. Those threat items suggest assault/combat-style danger expectations not otherwise represented in memory or appraisals.

issues.item: Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
issues.explanation: 'Stay near exit' similarly implies fear of immediate external danger or needing rapid escape from unsafe environments. In this profile, maladaptive strategies are otherwise distraction/substance-use based, and the core appraisals/memories are moral injury/guilt/shame focused; this specific escape-safety behavior is not well supported by the other selected items or trauma type.

vignette: Malia, a 43-year-old physical therapist, still cannot piece together the minutes before the accident. She remembers the warmth of the wine at the happy hour with colleagues, then the wet road, a cyclist appearing too close, the thud. What she cannot recall is whether she actually braked or froze. The police report said she was under the limit, but that fact brings no relief. What stays with her is the smell of alcohol on her own breath afterward, and the guilt that she had been drinking at all—that she had not done more to stop herself from getting behind the wheel. Having concluded that she was someone who could not be trusted to keep others safe, she began to see potential dangers everywhere—a cyclist on the street, a patient's sudden wince, the glint of a knife in the break room—as if the world had become full of chances for her to fail again. The cyclist survived but with severe brain trauma, and Malia now treats patients with similar injuries at a rehabilitation clinic. The smell of alcohol—whether from a patient’s mouth, a cleaning wipe, or the hand sanitizer at the clinic entrance—hits her like a punch. It triggers an immediate rush of shame and a fragmented, hyper-real memory of the impact, the way the man’s head hit the pavement. After that memory surfaced, she found that even the most ordinary things—a door slamming, a kettle whistling, the squeak of rubber on a clinic floor—now felt like warnings she could not afford to ignore. She has learned to avoid these moments: she holds her breath when passing the hand sanitizer dispenser, and she changes the subject whenever a coworker mentions car accidents. But each time she avoided, her nervous system logged it as proof that the threat was real and ongoing, keeping her hypervigilance locked in place. But the avoidance itself deepens her belief that she cannot handle thinking about the event, which makes the next trigger feel even more dangerous. When a trigger does break through, she notices every sharp object in the room—scissors, needles, even the legs of a metal chair—as though she is bracing for another catastrophe. Those threat-saturated moments, in turn, pull her back into the memory: the wet thud, the silence, the shame of not having a clear story. She has tried to numb the cycle by taking her neighbor’s leftover painkillers and by spending impulsively on online shopping, but each purchase or pill leaves her feeling even more unrecognizable to herself. She berates herself: *I am not the person I used to be.* That conviction—that she was fundamentally altered by the accident—kept pulling her back into the fragmented memory of the impact, as if locating her failure precisely might undo it. That self-appraisal then sharpens her vigilance—she scans for hazards everywhere, because surely she must be ready to prevent another disaster. The scanning itself becomes a trigger: a patient wincing during therapy, the smell of alcohol on a visitor’s breath, a coworker talking about a fender bender. The loop tightens. Malia also finds herself staying close to the exit during staff meetings, her chair always nearest the door. When she notices a pair of scissors on the counter, her heart races, and she feels the flashback coming—the cyclist’s helmetless head, the blood, her own paralyzed hands. The threat of her own emotional avalanche drives her to leave the room, or to take a drug to blunt the edge. Living at this pitch of constant threat, she had come to believe that she was permanently broken—that this was simply who she now was. But the drug use later amplifies her shame, reinforcing her belief that she is beyond forgiveness. She has stopped socializing with colleagues, and her partner has complained that she is distant and distracted. What finally brought her to seek help was a morning when she stood in the clinic, smelling hand sanitizer, and felt the memory surge with such force that she could not move. She realized she can no longer contain the cycle. She is terrified that talking about the accident will break her completely, but she is also terrified of continuing as she is—a stranger to herself, spending money she does not have, checking the exits, and waiting for the next trigger to find her. Already running on that sense of danger, almost anything could tip into a warning—a patient clearing their throat, a car horn outside, the squeak of a door hinge.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals directly drive the intrusive memory; memory is triggered by external cues or threat.
The vignette does not show that negative appraisals directly cause the perception of triggers; appraisals lead to hypervigilance, which then creates triggers, but not a direct causal link.
The vignette does not show that the trauma memory itself generates new triggers; triggers are repeatedly shown to prompt the memory, not the reverse.
The vignette does not show that the sense of threat directly produces negative appraisals; threat leads to maladaptive coping, and appraisals arise from that coping or from triggers.
The vignette does not show that the sense of threat directly causes the emergence of triggers; threat leads to scanning, which becomes a trigger, but no direct causation.

The vignette does not show that maladaptive strategies directly increase the sense of threat; avoidance deepens beliefs that make triggers feel more dangerous, but that route goes through negative appraisals.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals directly drive the intrusive memory; memory is triggered by external cues or threat.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals directly cause the perception of triggers; appraisals lead to hypervigilance, which then creates triggers, but not a direct causal link.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not show that the trauma memory itself generates new triggers; triggers are repeatedly shown to prompt the memory, not the reverse.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not show that the sense of threat directly produces negative appraisals; threat leads to maladaptive coping, and appraisals arise from that coping or from triggers.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette does not show that the sense of threat directly causes the emergence of triggers; threat leads to scanning, which becomes a trigger, but no direct causation.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not show that maladaptive strategies directly increase the sense of threat; avoidance deepens beliefs that make triggers feel more dangerous, but that route goes through negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."
